examples.before_answer: The opponent proposes a four-week trial on Fridays until 8:00 PM, contingent on named volunteers being present and prohibiting amplified sound. While the proposal includes a fallback to close at existing times if no volunteer is present, and commits to publishing neighbor complaints after the trial, these measures do not resolve our core concerns. Prohibiting amplified sound does not prevent other noise disturbances, such as shouting or heavy footsteps. Furthermore, a named volunteer is not a trained professional capable of managing conflicts or ensuring immediate neighbor protection. Recording complaints only after the trial concludes provides no real-time mitigation for residents. These constraints address the symptoms of potential disruption but leave the underlying execution gaps regarding noise monitoring and active security unaddressed.
examples.after_answer: The opponent proposes a four-week trial on Fridays until 8:00 PM, including a prohibition on amplified sound and a requirement for a named volunteer at each session. They also commit to recording and publishing neighbor complaints at the end of the trial. While these measures address certain concerns, they leave significant risks unresolved. Relying on a fallback to existing closing times if no volunteer is present may lead to inconsistent availability for users. Furthermore, documenting complaints after the trial concludes is a reactive measure; it does not prevent potential noise disturbances from occurring during the extended hours. We should seek proactive protections rather than relying on post-trial reports. Consequently, these safeguards may not sufficiently mitigate the risks of an unstable trial and potential neighborhood disturbance.
